title: Microsoft 365 Security Checklist
blurb: Identity and MFA, Conditional Access, admin roles, email security (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, forwarding), devices, audit logging and backups, each check with a Microsoft Learn link.
intro: A tenant-wide security baseline for Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Entra ID, taken from Microsoft’s own guidance. Work through it top to bottom; some checks need Entra ID P1 or P2, Intune or Defender for Office 365 licences, as noted in the linked pages.

items.check: Require multifactor authentication for every user, with security defaults or a Conditional Access policy.
items.why: MFA blocks the large majority of password-spray and credential-stuffing attacks against cloud accounts.

items.check: Require phishing-resistant MFA (passkeys/FIDO2, Windows Hello for Business or certificates) for administrators.
items.why: Admin accounts are the main target of adversary-in-the-middle phishing, which can relay app and SMS codes.

items.check: Enable self-service password reset for all users.
items.why: Users can recover from a forgotten or compromised password with verified methods instead of a helpdesk call.

items.check: Use Microsoft Entra Password Protection, with a custom banned-password list for your company and product names.
items.why: It rejects weak and commonly guessed passwords when users set or change them.

items.check: Create two cloud-only emergency access (break-glass) accounts, protected with phishing-resistant MFA and monitored for sign-ins.
items.why: They keep you from being locked out of the tenant if Conditional Access or a federation provider fails.

items.check: Block legacy authentication protocols for all users.
items.why: Legacy protocols such as POP, IMAP and SMTP basic auth cannot do MFA, so attackers use them to bypass it.

items.check: Turn on sign-in risk and user risk policies (Entra ID P2).
items.why: Microsoft Entra ID Protection can then demand MFA or a secure password change when a sign-in or account looks compromised.

items.check: Require a compliant or hybrid-joined device for access to company data.
items.why: Stolen credentials alone are no longer enough; the sign-in must come from a managed, healthy device.

items.check: Test every new policy in report-only mode before you enforce it, and exclude your emergency access accounts.
items.why: Report-only mode shows who a policy would affect, so you do not lock out users or yourself.

items.check: Restrict user consent to applications (verified publishers and low-risk permissions only) and set up the admin consent workflow.
items.why: Consent phishing tricks users into granting a malicious app ongoing access to mail and files.

items.check: Keep the number of Global Administrators small (Microsoft recommends fewer than five) and use dedicated, cloud-only admin accounts.
items.why: Every Global Administrator can change anything in the tenant, so each extra one widens the attack surface.

items.check: Assign the least-privileged role for each task, such as Exchange, User or Helpdesk Administrator, instead of Global Administrator.
items.why: A compromised account with a narrow role can do far less damage.

items.check: Use Privileged Identity Management for just-in-time, time-limited and approved role activation (Entra ID P2).
items.why: Standing admin access is replaced by roles that are active only when needed and are fully audited.

items.check: Publish an SPF record that lists every service allowed to send mail for your domains.
items.why: Receiving servers use SPF to check that mail claiming to be from your domain came from an authorised source.

items.check: Turn on DKIM signing for each custom domain in Microsoft 365.
items.why: DKIM signs outgoing mail so receivers can verify it was not altered and really came from your domain.

items.check: Publish a DMARC record, start with p=none and reporting, then move to quarantine or reject.
items.why: DMARC tells receivers what to do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM, which stops direct spoofing of your domain.

items.check: Block automatic forwarding to external addresses in the outbound spam policy, with exceptions only where needed.
items.why: Attackers who take over a mailbox often add a forwarding rule to copy mail out quietly.

items.check: Apply the Standard or Strict preset security policies for anti-spam, anti-phishing, Safe Links and Safe Attachments.
items.why: Presets keep protection at Microsoft’s recommended settings as new controls are added.

items.check: Enrol devices in Intune and set compliance policies (OS version, encryption, firewall, antivirus).
items.why: Compliance status is what Conditional Access uses to decide whether a device is trusted.

items.check: Use app protection policies for Outlook, Teams and OneDrive on personal phones.
items.why: They protect company data inside the apps (no copy to personal apps, PIN, selective wipe) without enrolling the phone.

items.check: Encrypt Windows devices with BitLocker and escrow the recovery keys in Entra ID.
items.why: A lost or stolen laptop then does not expose the files stored on it.

items.check: Confirm that Microsoft Purview audit (the unified audit log) is turned on.
items.why: Without the audit log you cannot investigate who read, changed or deleted mail and files.

items.check: Send Entra sign-in and audit logs to a Log Analytics workspace or your SIEM.
items.why: Entra keeps these logs for a limited time only; exporting them keeps the history you need for an investigation.

items.check: Review the default alert policies and send alerts to a monitored mailbox.
items.why: Built-in alerts flag events such as new forwarding rules, elevated mail sending and admin changes.

items.check: Check Microsoft Secure Score every month and work through its top recommended actions.
items.why: Secure Score measures your configuration against Microsoft’s recommendations and shows what to fix next.

items.check: Set retention policies for Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams that match your legal and business needs.
items.why: Retention keeps content for a set period even if a user deletes it.

items.check: Decide whether you need a backup in addition to retention, such as Microsoft 365 Backup or a third-party service, and test a restore.
items.why: Retention is not a point-in-time backup; a backup lets you roll back after ransomware or a bad bulk change.

title: Azure Cost Saving Checklist
blurb: Reservations and savings plans, rightsizing, orphaned disks, IPs and snapshots, dev/test schedules, storage tiers, egress, Log Analytics retention, tagging and budgets, each with a Microsoft Learn link.
intro: Practical cost checks for an Azure subscription, taken from Microsoft’s Cost Management, Advisor and Well-Architected guidance. Start with the items that match your largest cost lines in Cost analysis.

items.check: Open Cost analysis and group cost by service, resource group and resource for the last full month.
items.why: You need to know your largest cost lines before you decide which savings are worth the effort.

items.check: Work through the cost recommendations in Azure Advisor.
items.why: Advisor flags underused VMs, idle resources and reservation opportunities based on your actual usage.

items.check: Buy Azure Reservations for VMs, databases and other services that run steadily all year.
items.why: A one- or three-year commitment is charged at a significant discount to pay-as-you-go prices.

items.check: Use an Azure savings plan for compute when your workloads change size, region or service.
items.why: A savings plan applies an hourly spend commitment across eligible compute services, so it stays useful as things change.

items.check: Apply Azure Hybrid Benefit to Windows Server and SQL Server workloads covered by eligible licences.
items.why: You stop paying for a licence you already own through Software Assurance or a subscription.

items.check: Check reservation utilisation every month and exchange or resize reservations that are underused.
items.why: An unused reservation hour is lost money, because a reservation is billed whether or not it is used.

items.check: Resize or shut down VMs with consistently low CPU and memory use.
items.why: Many VMs are sized for a peak that never comes, and each size step down roughly halves compute cost.

items.check: Use autoscale for App Service, VM scale sets and other services with variable load.
items.why: Autoscale adds instances at peak and removes them when demand falls, so you do not pay for peak capacity all day.

items.check: Run interruptible batch, test and CI work on Azure Spot VMs.
items.why: Spot VMs use spare capacity at a deep discount, in exchange for possible eviction.

items.check: Check the disk type of each VM: move to Standard SSD where Premium SSD performance is not needed.
items.why: Premium SSD costs more per disk every month, whether or not its extra performance is used.

items.check: Find and delete unattached managed disks.
items.why: A managed disk is billed for its full provisioned size even after the VM using it has been deleted.

items.check: Release public IP addresses that are not associated with any resource.
items.why: Public IP addresses are billed by the hour while they exist, whether or not anything uses them.

items.check: Review old disk snapshots, delete the ones you no longer need and use incremental snapshots.
items.why: Full snapshots are billed for the whole disk size, while incremental snapshots store only the changes.

items.check: Deallocate VMs you stop, rather than only shutting them down from inside the operating system.
items.why: A VM that is stopped but still allocated keeps being billed for compute.

items.check: Delete empty or idle App Service plans.
items.why: An App Service plan is billed for its instances even when no app runs in it.

items.check: Set auto-shutdown schedules on dev and test VMs.
items.why: Machines used only in working hours do not need to run, and bill, through nights and weekends.

items.check: Run non-production subscriptions on Dev/Test pricing offers where your Visual Studio subscriptions allow it.
items.why: Dev/Test offers give discounted rates, including no Windows licence charge on VMs, for non-production use.

items.check: Move rarely read blobs to the cool, cold or archive access tier.
items.why: Cooler tiers cost much less per GB to store, with higher access costs and minimum storage periods.

items.check: Add lifecycle management rules that tier or delete blobs by age automatically.
items.why: Rules keep the tiering going without anyone having to remember it.

items.check: Use locally redundant storage (LRS) where geo-redundancy is not required.
items.why: Geo-redundant options store extra copies in a second region and cost more per GB.

items.check: Keep chatty services and their data in the same region and cut unneeded cross-region and internet data transfer.
items.why: Data leaving a region or Azure is billed per GB, while inbound transfer is free.

items.check: Set table-level retention to what you actually need and use long-term retention for data you keep only for compliance.
items.why: Retention beyond the included period is billed per GB per month.

items.check: Use the Basic or Auxiliary table plan for high-volume logs you rarely query, and a commitment tier if you ingest steadily.
items.why: Ingestion is usually the largest Log Analytics cost, and these options price it lower.

items.check: Set a daily cap on workspaces where a runaway data source could cause a surprise bill.
items.why: The cap stops billable ingestion for the rest of the day once the limit is reached.

items.check: Require cost-centre, owner and environment tags with Azure Policy.
items.why: Tags let you split the bill by team and find who owns an expensive resource.

items.check: Create budgets with email alerts at 50%, 80% and 100% for each subscription or resource group.
items.why: Budgets warn you during the month, before an overrun reaches the invoice.

items.check: Turn on anomaly alerts and review unexpected charges as soon as they are flagged.
items.why: Cost anomaly detection spots sudden spikes, such as a misconfigured scale rule, within days.
